rows: Records the page engine fixes the developer asked for during the grill of this ticket. They were built by hand on this branch and are committed; the build does not repeat them.
Already built and committed on this branch during the grill; it stands in the plan only so the build does not repeat it.
The forge port answers every change whose source is a given branch, with its state, on GitHub and GitLab, so gc can prove that at least one change merged and none is open.
The forge port is its own module with its own tests, and the refusal checks need its new verb first.

The gc target: one JSON file per feature branch in git's common folder, its encoded key, its atomic write, the Windows byte lock of one run per target, and the receipt of a list. Also the scratch repository the gc tests share.
The target file, its lock and its receipt are one module that every gc step uses, so it comes before them, with the shared scratch repository.
Removes one worktree folder only after a rename proves no process uses it, reads a refused rename's Windows error as its cause, and resumes a delete that stopped half way.
The rename check is the riskiest piece (real Windows processes hold folders), so it gets its own module and tests, apart from git and the forge.

One check per refusal of the PRD catalog: the forge state of the branch's changes, uncommitted and untracked files, commits outside the change, and the platform, each with the detail the developer sees.
Each refusal is a check with its own detail; keeping them in one module lets list, remove and finish run the same checks.

The gc script's first step: in the feature worktree it fixes the target, runs every check, and answers the list the developer says yes to, with its receipt. From elsewhere it only shows a waiting target.
The list is the step the developer says yes to; it can be built and tested before anything is deleted.

The gc script's second step: after the developer's yes it checks everything again, compares the receipt, and removes the run worktree, the run branch and the remote branches in order, recording what is left.
The deletes after the yes carry the most cases (order, lease, partial failure, rerun), so they get a sitting of their own.
The gc script's third step, which the developer runs after the session closes: it removes the feature worktree and the local feature branch, and deletes the target once nothing is left.
The developer's later command runs outside the session and needs no forge call, a separate step with its own refusals.

The /afkv2:gc skill that runs the 3 steps with the developer, the 'never run gc' line of the hands-off skills, 2 glossary terms, README.md on the ownership list, and the README section on gc and the platform.
The skill and every instruction or document line come once the script works, and are all text changes of one kind.

The CI watch ends when the change merges or closes, from the change view it already reads, and the create-change-request skill offers gc on a merged change: at the watch end, on the mark-ready refusal, and once at the end of ship.
The CI watch rework and the offer of gc live in another skill (create-change-request), and need the gc skill to exist.

A script the developer runs once per forge before merge: it makes scratch branches, merges a change into a scratch target, runs gc list, remove and finish, checks what is gone and what stays, checks that a deleted branch's commit link still opens, and deletes its scratch branches.
The live proof on GitHub and GitLab needs the whole gc script, and its run belongs to the developer, not to a hands-off build.

The code does what it was designed to do: a sign-off card counts as signed only by a sign mark with no note on that card, so any note, even a question, sends the card back.
